extracted.intended_audience: registered patent attorneys/agents, legal counsel, and USPTO OED staff involved in USPTO disciplinary/reciprocal-discipline matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedure for imposing reciprocal discipline on a registered practitioner under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d), including the Selling v. Radford framework, burdens of proof, and the types of evidence or defects that will prevent imposition of identical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal-discipline default rule under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact, that one of the listed Selling elements applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process; there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not accept the conclusion as final; the imposition of the same discipline by the Office would result in a grave injustice; or the practitioner was not publicly censured/reprimanded/placed on probation/disbarred/suspended/disciplinarily disqualified. Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly disciplined must be supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner's burden: clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent seeking to avoid imposition of reciprocal discipline must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal/USPTO review is narrow; the respondent bears the burden and must produce clear-and-convincing proof of a genuine issue of material fact (citing In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave-injustice inquiry (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Grave injustice is shown if the severity of the punishment does not 'fit' the misconduct — i.e., the punishment imposed by the state was so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that imposing the same discipline federally would be unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court looks to whether the state sanction was within the appropriate range of sanctions for the misconduct (citing cases such as In re Thav, In re Kramer, Matter of Benjamin). Respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence that the sanction was outside acceptable ranges; case law and state sanctioning standards (e.g., Florida Standards) inform the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due-process deprivation standard (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(1)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: To defeat reciprocal discipline on due-process grounds, a respondent must show the state procedure was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires 'the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner' (citing Mathews v. Eldridge, In re Karten). In disciplinary contexts, reasonable notice of charges, chance to present evidence, testify, call and cross-examine witnesses, and make argument satisfy due process (citing In re Ruffalo, In re Squire, In re Zdravkovich). Mere disagreement with a state's application of precedent does not establish a due-process deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof standard (Selling element)
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may avoid reciprocal discipline if there was such an infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept the conclusion as final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high threshold; respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence that the state record's proof is so deficient that the USPTO cannot accept the findings. The USPTO gives deference to the state's adjudication absent compelling proof of insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions — Section 3 factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing sanctions, a referee (and reviewing tribunal) should generally consider: (a) the duty violated; (b) the lawyer's mental state; (c) the potential or actual injury caused by the lawyer's misconduct; and (d) the existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors inform whether a particular sanction (e.g., disbarment) is appropriate and are applied in state proceedings; USPTO assesses whether the state applied these standards in determining whether reciprocal discipline is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6.11 standards for dishonesty/fraud/misrepresentation (disbarment triggers)
rubrics_metrics.description: For conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation to a court, disbarment is appropriate when (a) with intent to deceive the court, a lawyer knowingly makes a false statement or submits a false document; or (b) a lawyer improperly withholds material information and causes serious or potentially serious injury to a party, or causes a significant or potentially significant adverse effect on the legal proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referee/state court must make the required findings under Section 6.11(a) and/or (b) for disbarment to be within the justified range; USPTO will consider whether those findings were made when evaluating grave-injustice and proof infirmity claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of disciplinary proceedings (remedial, not criminal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney disciplinary proceedings are primarily remedial — aimed to protect the public and administration of justice — and thus the Double Jeopardy Clause does not apply to bar imposition of reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case law establishing disciplinary proceedings' remedial purpose (e.g., Chastain, Matter of Caranchini, In re Jaffe) and explains that arguments based on double jeopardy are inapposite in disciplinary contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to state referee findings and credibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will give weight to state-level findings, including referee credibility determinations, unless the respondent can clearly and convincingly show a genuine issue of material fact under Selling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: where the referee observed testimony and found it not credible and applied the applicable standards (Sections 3 and 6.11), the USPTO will accept those findings absent compelling contrary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial and administrative orders upon federal reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: If reciprocal discipline is imposed, the USPTO will issue orders including exclusion from practice before the USPTO, publication of notice in the Official Gazette, notice to state disciplinary agencies and courts, dissociation of the practitioner's name from Customer Numbers and PKI certificates, and prohibition on obtaining or being added to a Customer Number until reinstated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order may specify the effective date of exclusion, require OED Director to give notice pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.59, and list sources where disciplinary decisions are publicly available (e.g., OED Reading Room). Review of the final decision is available by petition to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.57(a).
